title: Weak Ties, Small Worlds & Tipping Boards — Mark Granovetter's 1973 Strength of Weak Ties (83.4% Job Bridges & Forbidden Triad), Watts & Strogatz's 1998 Small-World Rewiring (p = 0.01), Thomas Schelling's 1971 Checkerboard Tipping & Threshold Cascades, and SARS-CoV-2 Spike–ACE2 Percolation (PDB 6VYB, 6M0J, 7T9L)

teenKit.tldr: Tiny local interactions—like moving a penny on a checkerboard or meeting an old acquaintance—can trigger massive, system-wide social, urban, or biological cascades. Network geometry completely breaks the rule that big changes require massive forces.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Understanding how small-world networks and weak ties operate explains everything from how you will land your future job to how viral outbreaks and neighborhood segregation sweep across populations.
keyTakeaways: Mark Granovetter's research proved that weak ties (acquaintances rather than close friends) act as crucial job bridges because they connect completely different social circles.
Thomas Schelling demonstrated through checkerboard models that even mild personal preferences can snowball into complete racial or social segregation through threshold cascades.
At the molecular level, microscopic weak ties between viral spike proteins and human cells dictate the scale and severity of a global pandemic.

vocab.meaning: Superficial connections with acquaintances that bridge separate social clusters, offering fresh information and opportunities that close friends cannot provide.
A graph structure where most nodes are not neighbors of one another, but most nodes can be reached from every other node by a small number of steps.
A phenomenon where a local shift or small action triggers a domino effect that rapidly transforms an entire macro-system.
The process by which a substance or infection spreads through a network by finding connected pathways from node to node.

quiz.question: According to Mark Granovetter's 1973 study, why are weak ties so much more effective than strong ties when finding a new job?
options: Close friends keep all job openings a secret from you.
Weak ties act as bridges to entirely different social circles, introducing novel information you wouldn't otherwise hear.
Employers prefer candidates who have fewer friends.
Weak ties are legally required to help people find employment.
quiz.explanation: Weak ties connect isolated clusters of people, allowing information to travel across structural holes into your personal network.

quiz.question: What did Thomas Schelling's 1971 checkerboard model reveal about human behavior and neighborhood segregation?
options: Cities only segregate when governments pass strict zoning laws.
People always prefer to live completely isolated from everyone else.
Even mild, non-hostile preferences about neighbors can cascade into total macro-segregation.
Random movement always leads to perfectly integrated communities.
quiz.explanation: Schelling proved that micro-motives (slight preferences for similar neighbors) easily generate macro-behavior (total segregation).

quiz.question: How do small-world networks challenge traditional physical intuition about cause and effect?
options: They prove that massive changes require massive, heavy-handed forces to happen.
They show that the geometry of connections allows tiny local nudges to ignite massive system-wide cascades.
They demonstrate that networks are completely random and impossible to model mathematically.
They show that distance is the only factor that matters in human relationships.
quiz.explanation: Network topology breaks the proportional logic of physics, showing that microscopic inputs can cause macroscopic revolutions.
